answer.rationale:
The binding constraints are that the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days. That ordering matters: an 18% spend mandate is a cost target, but a supply gap or migration stumble in a 14-day window is an unrecoverable delivery failure. So I want the cheapest path that touches the physical flow of parts least, and that is renegotiating the existing contract rather than moving primary supply.

Why verify memory_c4 and memory_c2. memory_c4 is the memory my intended action rests on entirely — it claims benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and terms. I need the original record to see the actual magnitude recovered, because if it was 3-5% it does not reach an 18% mandate and I am choosing a comfortable action that quietly fails the objective. memory_c2 is the strongest competing pull: it is the only memory that credibly promises a sharp unit-cost cut, which is exactly what finance is asking for. That makes it the most dangerous inherited claim in the set, so it earns scrutiny rather than deference. Its language is outcome-only — cheap, fast onboarding, accurate invoicing — with nothing about on-time delivery, yield, or behavior under load. It is also stamped "last year," and it does not say whether that switch happened with slack in the line or with zero buffer as we have now. An unqualified success summary written after the fact is the shape a survivorship record takes; I want the source before letting a cost number pull me into a primary-vendor migration.

The general hazard: every one of these six memories reads as a win. That is not evidence that every direction works here, it is evidence that the consolidation step kept outcomes and dropped context and failures. I am treating them as reliable about what happened, not as transferable to a 14-day window with no buffer.

Guarded scale means: renegotiate as a short extension with benchmarked pricing, not the multi-year lock-in memory_c6 recommends. memory_c6's volume pricing is real but it buys a discount by spending exactly the option value I need most right now — if the incumbent underperforms, or if the low-cost vendor in memory_c2 checks out on delivery, I want to be able to act next cycle. Downstream risk I am flagging explicitly: the cost figures in memory_c2 and memory_c4 will be read by whoever inherits this as settled facts, and if I commit against a number I never sourced, that error compounds and hardens. Also flagging that if negotiation lands short of 18%, the residual gap goes to the next review as an open item, not as something I paper over — and memory_c3's second-source play stays queued there, since single-point-of-failure exposure is unaddressed by this decision and remains a live risk rather than a solved one.
